Chromosome Arrangements at Metaphase of Meiosis I

4 chromosomes

2 pairs

Text description of this image

Two equally probable arrangements of chromosomes at metaphase of meiosis 1.; Parent Cell with 2 pairs of duplicated homologous chromosomes (long and short). Homologous pairs line up at the middle of the cell to be separated.; Possibility 1: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids; long maternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids; Possibility 2: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids; long maternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids; Metaphase of meiosis 2:; 2 daughter cells each with one long and one short set of sister chromatids; Possibility 1

§ Cell 1: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids in middle of cell. § Cell 2: Long maternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids in the center of cell.

Possibility 2:

§ Cell 1: Long paternal sister chromatids line up above short maternal sister chromatids in the middle of cell. § Cell 2: long maternal sister chromatids line up above short paternal sister chromatids in middle of cell.

Gametes; 4 haploid daughter cells show four combinations of gametes. Because possibilities one and two (alignment at metaphase I) are equally likely, the four possible types of gametes will be made in approximately equal numbers.; Possibility 1: Combination a (2 cells): Long paternal chromosome and short paternal chromosome. Combination b (2 cells): Long maternal chromosome and short maternal chromosome.; Possibility 2: Combination c (2 cells): long paternal chromosome, short maternal chromosome. Combination d (2 cells): short paternal chromosome, long maternal chromosome.

Text description of this image

The figure shows that each homologous pair consists of chromosomes of the same length and with matching color bands (with the exception of the X and Y chromosomes; the Y chromosome is much shorter than X and does not have matching color bands). An exploded drawing of homologous chromosomes (pair 1) shows that each member of the pair is a duplicated chromosome, which consists of sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

Genetics and Heredity

  • Heredity is the transmission of traits from one generation to the next.
  • Genetics is the scientific study of heredity.
  • Gregor Mendel worked in the 1860s and found that

Mendel and the Pea Plants

  • A character is a heritable feature that varies among individuals.
    • A trait is a variant of a character.
    • Each of the characters Mendel studied occurred in two distinct traits.
  • Perhaps the most important advantage of pea plants as an experimental model was that Mendel could strictly control their reproduction.
Text description of this image

A photo shows a pea flower. The petals surround the reproductive structures, which include the thick carpel (produces eggs) surrounded by long, thin stamens (make sperm-producing pollen).

  • Hybrids are the offspring of two different purebred varieties.
    • The cross-fertilization itself is referred to as a genetic cross.
    • The parental plants are the P generation.
    • Their hybrid offspring are the F1 generation.
    • A cross of the F1 plants forms the F2 generation.
Text description of this image

The figure shows both the Parents (P) and the Offspring (F1) generations. Mendel removed stamens from a purple pea flower in the parent generation; in the drawing, the stamens are removed using scissors. Using a brush, he then transferred pollen from the stamens of a white flower to the carpel of the purple flower. The pollinated carpel matured into a pod. He planted the seeds (peas) from the pod, which grew up into the offspring (F1 generation). All of the flowers on the offspring plants are purple.

Inheritance of a single character

  • Mendel figured out that the gene for white flowers did not disappear in the F1 plants but was somehow hidden or masked when the purple-flower factor was present.
  • He also deduced that the F1 plants must have carried two factors for the flower-color character, one for purple and one for white.
Text description of this image

A black-and-white photo shows Gregor Mendel examining a sample. The figure shows that in the P generation (purebred parents), plants with purple flowers are crossed with plants with white flowers. Their offspring, the F1 generation, all have purple flowers. Fertilization among F1 plants (F1 cross F1) produces the F2 generation. In the F2 generation, three fourth of the plants have purple flowers, and one fourth have white flowers.

  • There are alternative versions of genes that account for variations in inherited characters.
  • For each inherited character, an organism inherits two alleles, one from each parent.
  • If an organism has two different alleles for a gene, one allele determines the organism’s appearance and is called the dominant allele; the other allele has no noticeable effect on the organism’s appearance and is called the recessive allele.
  • A sperm or egg carries only one allele for each inherited character because the two alleles for a character segregate (separate) from each other during the production of gametes.

Geneticists distinguish between an organism’s

physical appearance, its phenotype,

genetic makeup, its genotype.

Text description of this image

In the P generation, purple flowers are crossed with white flowers. The genetic makeup (alleles), carried by the parents are uppercase P uppercase P (for purple flowers) and lowercase p lowercase p (for white flowers). The purple-flowered plant produces gametes that are all uppercase P, while the white-flowered plant produces gametes that are all lowercase p.; In the F1 generation (hybrids), only purple flowers are produced, all of which have the genetic makeup uppercase P lowercase p. The alleles segregate such that ½ the gametes are uppercase P (purple allele) and ½ are lowercase p (white allele).; In the F2 generation (hybrids), a Punnett square shows the outcome of the cross.; Gametes: Uppercase P sperm from F1 plant and Lowercase p sperm from F1 plant; Uppercase P egg from F1 plant: Uppercase P uppercase P (purple flowers); Uppercase P lowercase p (purple flowers); Lowercase p egg from F1 plant: Uppercase P lowercase p (purple flowers); lowercase p lowercase p (white flowers); Phenotypic ratio: 3 purple: 1 white; Genotypic ratio: 1 uppercase P uppercase P: 2 uppercase P lowercase P: 1 lowercase p lowercase p

Relationship between Alleles and Homologous Chromosomes

  • A pair of homologous chromosomes—chromosomes that carry alleles of the same genes.
  • A gene locus is a specific location of a gene along a chromosome.
    • Alleles (alternative versions) of a gene reside at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
    • However, the two chromosomes may bear either identical alleles or different ones at any one locus.
Text description of this image

A pair of homologous chromosomes is shown with one maternal and one paternal chromosome. Three gene loci are mapped on the chromosomes, for genes P, A, and B. These loci are specific regions that match location on each chromosome in the homologous pair; each chromosome carries only one allele for each gene.; Uppercase versions of alleles are dominant; lowercase versions are recessive.; The maternal chromosome carries the alleles uppercase P, lowercase a, and uppercase B.; The paternal chromosome carries the alleles uppercase P, lowercase a, and lowercase b.; The genotype represented by this pair of homologous chromosomes is therefore uppercase P uppercase P (homozygous for the dominant allele); lowercase a lowercase a (homozygous for the recessive allele); and uppercase B lowercase b (heterozygous with one dominant and one recessive allele).

Family Pedigrees

  • Geneticists who study people obviously cannot control the mating of their research participants. Instead, they must analyze the results of mating that have already occurred.
    • First, a geneticist collects as much information as possible about a family’s history for a trait.
    • Then the researcher assembles this information into a family tree, called a pedigree.

Wild-type traits (those seen most often in nature) are not necessarily specified by dominant alleles.

Human Traits Controlled by a Single Gene

  • The genetic bases of many human characters, such as eye and hair color, are complex and poorly understood.
    • Mendel’s laws can be applied to the inheritance of human traits that are generally agreed to be determined by a single gene, such as freckles or a widow’s peak hairline.
Text description of this image

A photo shows a woman with a widow’s peak hairline as a dominant trait. A photo shows a woman with a straight hairline as a recessive trait.

Text description of this image

A table lists the major symptoms of a list of recessive and dominant disorders. The recessive disorders and their major symptoms are as follows:

Albinism: Lack of pigment in skin, hair, and eyes; the corresponding photo shows an albino person with white hair, pale skin, and eyes with a lack of color.; Cystic fibrosis: Excess mucus in lungs, digestive tract, liver; increased susceptibility to infections; death in early childhood unless treated; Phenylketonuria (PKU): Accumulation of phenylalanine in blood; lack of normal skin pigment; developmental disabilities unless treated; the corresponding photo shows a list of ingredients with “phenylketonurics: contains phenylalanine” highlighted.; Sickle-cell disease: Misshapen red blood cells; damage to many tissues; the corresponding photo shows a sickled red blood cell.; Tay-Sachs disease: Lipid accumulation in brain cells; developmental deficiencies; death in childhood; The dominant disorders and their major symptoms are as follows:; Achondroplasia: Dwarfism; Alzheimer’s disease (one type): Mental deterioration; usually strikes late in life; the corresponding image shows an MRI of the brain.; Huntington’s disease: Uncontrollable movements; cognitive impairments; occurs in middle age; Hypercholesterolemia: Excess cholesterol in blood; heart disease.

Recessive Disorders

  • Most genetic mutations that cause medical disorders are recessive.
    • Individuals who have the recessive allele but appear normal are carriers of the disorder.

Dominant Disorders

  • A number of human disorders are caused by dominant alleles. An example is achondroplasia, a form of dwarfism in which the head and torso develop normally but the arms and legs are short.
    • The homozygous dominant genotype (AA) causes death of the embryo, and therefore only heterozygotes (Aa), individuals with a single copy of the defective allele, have this disorder.

Codominance & Multiple Alleles

Text description of this image

Each row is a blood group. Group A: genotype IAIA or IAi, red cells carry carbohydrate A, blood contains anti-B antibodies. Group B: genotype IBIB or IBi, carbohydrate B, anti-A antibodies. Group AB: genotype IAIB, carbohydrates A and B, no antibodies. Group O: genotype ii, no carbohydrates, anti-A and anti-B antibodies. Reactions when blood from groups O, A, B and AB is mixed with the antibodies at left: group A antibodies (anti-B) clump B and AB blood. Group B antibodies (anti-A) clump A and AB blood. Group AB has no antibodies, so nothing clumps. Group O antibodies (anti-A and anti-B) clump A, B and AB blood but not O blood.

Polygenic Inheritance

  • Polygenic inheritance is the additive effects of two or more genes on a single phenotypic character and the logical opposite of pleiotropy, in which one gene affects several characters.

Chromosomal Basis of Mendel’s Laws

Text description of this image

P generation: Round-yellow seeds (RRYY all uppercase) are crossed with wrinkled green seeds (rryy all lowercase). Drawings of each parent cell show that both contain four chromosomes, each carrying one of the four alleles. The chromosomes carrying R are long and the chromosomes carrying Y are short. During meiosis, the round-yellow parent makes all RY both uppercase gametes (alleles are on two different chromosomes; R on long and Y on short); the wrinkled-green parent makes all ry, both lowercase gametes (again, r and y are on separate chromosomes). Fertilization occurs between the gametes.; F1 generation: All yellow-round seeds (with genotype uppercase R lowercase r uppercase Y lowercase y). The alleles are on four separate chromosomes (two paternal and two maternal).; Law of segregation: Follow the long chromosomes (carrying uppercase R and lowercase r) taking either the right or left branch. Only one long chromosome ends up in each gamete.; Law of independent assortment: Follow both the long (R) and short (y) chromosomes. They are arranged in either of two equally likely ways at metaphase I. The chromosomes sort independently, giving four gamete types.; Start with F1 cell: round-yellow (uppercase R lowercase r uppercase Y lowercase y) cell; enters meiosis; Left branch: One possible alignment at metaphase I: The long maternal sister chromatids carrying uppercase R pair up with the long paternal sister chromatids carrying lowercase r at the center of the cell. The long maternal sister chromatids are lined up end to end with the short maternal sister chromatids; likewise the long paternal sister chromatids are lined up end to end with the short maternal sister chromatids; likewise the long paternal sister chromatids are lined up end to end with the short paternal sister chromatids. The uppercase R and lowercase r alleles segregate in anaphase I of meiosis (this also happens for the Y alleles). Two daughter cells result:

One daughter cell contains the long maternal sister chromatids carrying the uppercase R allele and the short maternal sister chromatids carrying the uppercase Y allele; enters metaphase II (only one long chromosome ends up in each gamete):

Gametes are ¼ RY both uppercase (two gametes each containing two maternal chromosomes, one with uppercase R and the other with uppercase Y)

The second daughter cell carries the long paternal sister chromatids with the lowercase r allele and the short paternal sister chromatids with the lowercase y allele; enters metaphase II (only one long chromosome ends up in each gamete):

Gametes are ¼ ry both lowercase (two gametes each containing two paternal chromosomes; one with lowercase r and one with lowercase y); Right branch: A second possible alignment during metaphase I: The long paternal sister chromatids carrying lowercase r pair up with the long maternal sister chromatids carrying uppercase R at the center of the cell. The short maternal sister chromatids carrying uppercase Y also pair up with the short paternal sister chromatids carrying lowercase y at the center of the cell. The long paternal sister chromatids are lined up end to end with the short maternal sister chromatids; likewise the long maternal sister chromatids line up end to end with the short paternal sister chromatids. Two daughter cells result:

One daughter cell contains the long paternal sister chromatids with the lowercase r allele and the short maternal sister chromatids with the uppercase Y allele; they sort independently, giving four gamete types following metaphase II:

Gametes are ¼ lowercase r uppercase Y (two gametes with the long paternal chromosome with lowercase r and short maternal chromosome with uppercase Y)

The second daughter cell contains the long maternal sister chromatids with the uppercase R allele and the short paternal sister chromatids with the lowercase y allele; they sort independently, giving four gamete types following metaphase II:

Gametes are ¼ uppercase R lowercase y (two gametes both containing the long maternal chromosome with uppercase R and the short paternal chromosome with lowercase y); Fertilization among the F1 plants: Fertilization recombines the lowercase r and uppercase R alleles at random and results in the 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation.; F2 generation: 9 round yellow seeds to 3 round green seeds to 3 wrinkled yellow seeds to 1 wrinkled green seed.

Sex Determining in Humans

  • Many animals, including all mammals, have a pair of sex chromosomes, designated X and Y, that determine an individual’s sex.
    • Individuals with one X chromosome and one Y chromosome are males.
    • XX individuals are females.
Text description of this image

The figure shows the somatic cells of a human male (shown in a photo) carry 44 chromosomes plus XY. The somatic cells of a human female (also pictured) carry 44 chromosomes plus XX. The man makes sperm, half that carry 22 plus X and half that carry 22 plus Y. All of the woman’s eggs carry 22 plus X. If the man’s 22 plus Y sperm fertilizes a woman’s egg, the offspring is 44 plus XY and is male. If the man’s 22 plus X sperm fertilizes a woman’s egg, the offspring is 44 plus XX and is female. Inset photographs are of a baby boy and a baby girl.

Sex-Linked Genes

  • A gene located on a sex chromosome is called a sex-linked gene. Most sex-linked genes are found on the X chromosome.
    • Several human conditions, including red-green colorblindness, hemophilia, and a type of muscular dystrophy, result from sex-linked recessive alleles.
    • Red-green colorblindness is a common sex-linked disorder caused by a malfunction of light-sensitive cells in the eyes. Mostly males are affected, but heterozygous females have some defects too.

Chapter Summary

  • Heredity is the transmission of traits from one generation to the next and genetics is the scientific study of heredity.
  • Mendel established four hypothesis that addressed the heredity of characters.
  • Some human traits are controlled by a single gene, but many characters are impacted by polygenic inheritance.
  • Most disorders will be recessive, but some can be dominant.
  • There are variations to Mendel’s Laws
  • There are conditions that are sex-linked
